full_judgment:
Abu Bakar Siddiquee J. This Jail Appeal is preferred against the judgment and order dated 06th November, 2012 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Death Reference No.46 of 2007 heard analogously with Jail Appeal No.700 of 2007 and. Criminal Appeal No.3726 of 2007 accepting the reference and dismissing the appeal so far it relates to the appellant and thus affirming the sentence of death awarded against him by the learned Judge of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal No.1, Rangpur in Nari-O-Shishu Case No.540 of 2002. 

 2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that the condemned prisoner, Md. Ismail Hossain, son of Md. Shafiullah of village-Nijhal, police station Mithapukur, District-Rangpur is the husband of victim, Most. Razia Begum (20) who entered into a marital tie about one year ago from the alleged date of occurrence dated 19.05.2002 and the victim while was residing with the condemned prison-er in the same bedroom was being slaughtered. Her dead body was found on the floor of the bedroom. 

 5. After receiving a written ejahar, the officer-in-charge of Mithapukur Police Station filled up the column of the FIR Form and recorded Mithapukur Police Station Case No.41 dated 20.05.2002. The task of investigation of the case was entrusted with Lokman Hossain, Sub-Inspector of Police, Mithapukur Police Station who visited the place of occurrence, prepared a sketch map of the place of occurrence, prepared an inquest report of the victim, sent the dead body of the victim to a morgue for autopsy, recorded statement of the witness under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, arrested the condemned prisoner on 17.07.2002 at about 5:00 pm from village Nayanpur and produced him at 1:00 pm on 18.07.2002 before Mr. Bashirul Alam, Magistrate, 1st class for recording his confessional statement. The condemned prisoner willfully confessed that he had killed the victim as he saw the victim taking part in illicit sexual intercourse with a young man who fled away. 

 7. Thereafter, the case record was transferred to Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal No.1, Rangpur for trial and was registered as Nari-O-Shishu Case No.540 of 2002. 

 10. The defence case of this appellant as it appears from the trend of cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses was that he never wanted dowry or never killed the victim on account of dowry. On the day of occurrence, the appellant, seeing his wife (the victim) having illicit sexual intercourse with another man, lost consciousness and killed the victim by slaughtering her with a Hasua (one kind of sharp cutting local weapon like a heavy scythe). 

 13. The learned Judge of the Tribunal submitted the proceedings or the case to the High Court Division under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 29 of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain which was registered as Death Reference No.46 of 2007. The appellant filed Jail Appeal No.700 of 2007 and Criminal Appeal No.3726 of 2007. A Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing the death reference along with the appeals, by the impugned judgment and order, accepted Death Reference No.46 of 2007 and dismissed Jail Appeal No.700 of 2007 and Criminal Appeal No.3726 of 2007. 

 15. Mr. ABM Bayzzid, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and the Court below misread and misconceived the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the aspects of the law and as such, there is a doubt to consider the convict appellant guilty in this case and the benefit of doubt be given to the condemned prisoner for the ends of justice. 

 16. Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the State, on the other hand, supports the impugned judgment contending that the instant case is one of the cold-blooded murders where the accused/murderer is none but the husband of the victim and admittedly the victim was residing with her husband's house under the custody of her husband. He further submits that the condemned prisoner was absconding since the date of occurrence till his arrest on 17.07.2005 and thereafter, the condemned prisoner voluntarily made a confessional statement before the First Class Magistrate which was recorded by observing all the legal formalities wherein the condemned prisoner admitted his guilt and equivocally admitted that he had slaughtered his wife while she was engaged with illicit sexual intercourse with another whom he did not know. The learned DAG also submits that the condemned prisoner could not mention the name of the person with whom the victim was allegedly engaged with illicit sexual intercourse because the said disclosure of engaging in illicit sexual intercourse was an afterthought development in the mind of the condemned prisoner to get rid of the charge leveled against him. He further submits that it was evident from the evidence of PWs, inquest report and post mortem report that the victim was often mentally and physically tortured by her husband for dowry and even just a day before the date of occurrence while the informant visited the house of the condemned prisoner to see her sister found some abrasion on the body of the victim and the victim disclosed that she was physically tortured by her husband for dowry which undoubtedly proved that the victim was killed by the condemned prisoner for dowry. He finally submits that since the prosecution has been able to prove the case beyond reasonable shadow of a doubt, the jail appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 18. In view of the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate in favour of condemned prisoners, we would like to refer relevant evidence and materials on record and scan attending facts and circumstances of this case to arrive at a proper decision. 

 30. It is a wife killing case where victim Most. Razia Begum (20) met her unnatural death at some point in the night following 19.05.2002 in. her husband's house when her husband, accused-appellant Md. Ismail Hossain, admittedly, remained present there. Thereafter, the accused-appellant with all the inmates of the house fled away from the spot but on 17.07.2002 the police arrested him. From the materials on record, it is evident that after arrest, the accused-appellant made a confessional statement before a First Class Magistrate under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Magistrate, after observing all the legal requirements, duly recorded his confessional statement where the accused-appellant confessed that he killed the victim by slaughtering her with a hasua. The accused-appellant, in his confession, also took the plea that he went to cut paddy at night and came back to his home at 2:00 AM and found his wife (the victim) having illicit sexual intercourse with another man, lost his consciousness, killed the victim by slaughtering her with a hasua (one kind of sharp cutting local weapon like a heavy scythe). 

 33. Ordinarily the accused has no obligation to account for the death for which he is placed for trial. But in the instant case, the murder of wife having taken place in presence of husband at dead hours of night, than the husband under section 106 of the Evidence Act is under obligation to explain how his wife has met with her death. We find that the husband offered an explanation to the effect that he killed his wife under tremendous provocation since his wife involved herself in illicit relation with another man at those dead hours of night. Now, it stands that the husband tried to take shelter under a plea of alifi to the effect that, he was under tremendous provocation which turned him in to a balance less mental condition and consciousness and in such a condition he offered hashua blow toward her wife who instantaneously met with her death. It is an acceptable proposition that it is the definite and specific defence being within the special knowledge of the condemned prisoner as such the burden is cast upon him to discharge it specially where, we find that the condemned prisoner himself implicated by making confessional statement. 

 34. 'Obligation to give an explanation' endorsed in the case of Abdul Motaleb Howlader Vs The State, reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 27 and Dipok Kumar Sarker Vs The State, reported in 40 DLR (AD) (1988) 139. 35. The learned. Deputy Attorney General in this regard referred a decision enunciated in the case of Mahabur Sheikh Vs. the State, 67 DLR (AD) (2015) page 54 wherein it has been held that:- 

 "It is by now well-established principle that under section 106 of the Evidence Act when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person the burden of proving that fact is upon him. This principle has been applied in may case where the wife has been found killed in the house of the husband where they reside together. . ."(sic) 

 38. In the instant case, the defence tried to suggest that the condemned prisoner's wife had an illicit relationship with another person but no iota of evidence was adduced in support of the suggestion, rather the said suggestion was vehemently denied by all the PWs. Moreover, the High Court Division rightly observed that without taking any step to catch red-handed the said man or raising his voice to call the help of others for arresting the said man, the condemned prisoner would not have slaughtered his wife straight-way. It also observed by the High Court Division that the act of slaughtering might have been done while the victim was sleeping because applying right to self defence is something intrinsic in every man and if the victim was alert at the time of the occurrence, she naturally must have tried to prevent or resist it by using her hands or other parts of her body and, if she tried, there would be the mark of injuries being used on her hands or any other parts of her body. Even, during examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 the condemned prisoner had an opportunity to explain the circumstances of the alleged fact of special knowledge, but he did not say anything rather pleaded not guilty. As a result, such a 'plea or explanation' remains an anecdote, not a fact. 

 40. Law is now well settled that confessional statement of an accused, if it is found true and voluntary, can be relied upon for the purpose of conviction, confessional statement of the condemned prisoner and no further corroboration is necessary and it can be the sole basis of the conviction and such view .finds sup-port from a case of this Division titled Islamuddin (Md) Din Islam Vs. the State reported in 13 BLC (AD) (2008) 81 wherein it has been held as follows:- 

 "It is now the settled principle of law that judicial confession if it is found to be true and voluntary can form the sole basis of conviction as against the maker of the same. The High Court Division as noticed earlier found the judicial confession of the condemned prisoner true and voluntary and, considering the same, the extra judicial confession and circumstances of the case, found the condemned prisoner guilty and accordingly imposed the sentence of death upon him." 

 41. There is complete chain of circumstances that the condemned prisoner slaughtered the deceased victim severely and dealt fatal blow causing her death which has been corroborated by the medical evidence and other circumstantial evidence of the case taken cumulatively which formed a chain so complete that there is no escape from the conclusion that the murder of victim was committed by the condemned prisoner and none else. 

 42. It appears that the High Court Division as noticed earlier found the judicial confession of the condemned prisoner true and voluntary and considering the same, the other evidence and circumstances of the case found that this condemned prisoner, Md. Ismail Hossain, intentionally murdered his wife, Most. Razia Begum, by slaughtering with a cold-blooded mind for the cause of dowry at his house, accepted the death reference and dismissed the jail appeal and the criminal appeal.
